86	### Type Definitions and Prescribed Treatments
87	
88	**physical law** — a constraint imposed by physics, mathematics, or formal logic that cannot change regardless of context or decisions made.
89	Prescribed treatment: accept as a ground-truth candidate and record it in the Ground Truths section.
90	
91	**current constraint** — a real limitation that applies now but could change (budget, team size, regulatory environment, technology availability).
92	Prescribed treatment: record the expiry conditions — what would have to change for this constraint to no longer hold. Do not treat it as permanent.
93	
94	**convention** — a practice or standard that exists because it has been adopted, not because it is physically or logically required.
95	Prescribed treatment: explicitly challenge the convention before accepting it. "We do it this way" is not a justification.
96	
97	**untested belief** — a claim held as true that has not been empirically verified in the context of this analysis.
98	Prescribed treatment: verify it, or flag it unverified. An untested belief used in a derivation chain must be marked with the `GT-N?` notation (see Ground Truths) and any conclusion depending on it inherits a confidence caveat.
99	
100	### Stakes-Escalation Rule
101	
102	The higher the stakes of the conclusion resting on an assumption, the more that assumption must be pushed toward physical law or verified ground truth status. Classification drives the method — it does not merely label.

104	### Verdict Vocabulary
105	
106	The Verdict cell is a token prefix followed by an em-dash and the justification — the bare
107	token leads so it stays matchable, and the em-dash prose carries the reasoning. **The separator
108	is an em-dash, never a colon.** `Accept: the figure is audited` puts the token and the reasoning
109	on one side of a punctuation mark that appears throughout ordinary prose, so the cell stops being
110	matchable — which is the whole property the token-first form exists to provide. Measured: a single
111	run using the colon form scored ten non-conforming verdict cells at once. The em-dash is not a
112	stylistic preference here; it is the delimiter:
113	
114	- **Accept** — the assumption survives challenge and may be used in the analysis (e.g., "Accept — survives P2 challenge; physical-law backed by GT-1")
115	- **Challenge** — the assumption is questionable; probe further before use (e.g., "Challenge — vendor benchmark unverified, flagged GT-5?")
116	- **Discard** — the assumption is false or irrelevant; remove from the reasoning chain (e.g., "Discard — contradicted by GT-2, no longer load-bearing")

118	**A current-constraint verdict records its expiry at the point of use.** An assumption classified `current constraint` is accepted only until that constraint lapses; the verdict cell says when. The expiry belongs in the em-dash justification and never in the token slot — the token slot carries one of the three tokens above and nothing else.

175	
176	Show how the ground truths combine into conclusions. Every conclusion offered in this analysis must have exactly one chain here — no more (no redundant restatement), no fewer (no orphaned conclusions).
177	
178	**Chain numbering convention.** Number each `### Conclusion:` block in this section `C1`,
179	`C2`, ... in document order (e.g., `### Conclusion C1: [Conclusion text]`). The §6→§4
180	closure ledger (the agent body — `SKILL.md` on the skill surface, `agents/first-principles.md` on the agent surface — "Before presenting conclusions") cites these IDs when mapping a

183	**Chain format:**
184	
185	```text
186	GT-N + GT-M → [intermediate claim] → [conclusion]
187	```
188	
189	The one-line form is the degenerate case, used only when the whole chain fits on one physical line; a chain that does not fit uses the head-plus-arrow-led form, and a hop is split rather than continued on a second line.
190	
191	Each chain must contain at least one intermediate step. A chain that goes directly from its head inputs to conclusion is incomplete — the intermediate is where the reasoning happens. The intermediate must be a new claim that could not be stated from any single head input alone. If no intermediate can be stated, the conclusion is either a restatement of a head input (trivial) or a reasoning step is missing.
192	
193	**No-wrap rule.** A hop occupies exactly one physical line. Every line after the head begins with `→` and carries exactly one complete hop; a hop is never broken across physical lines. A chain needing more hops continues on further arrow-led lines. A hop too long for comfort is SPLIT, not wrapped — the analysis renders as Markdown, so a long hop soft-wraps for the reader without breaking the form.

195	```text

197	→ [intermediate claim]
198	→ [further intermediate]
199	→ [conclusion]

201	
202	**Head-input rule.** The head line lists the inputs the chain consumes: each is a `GT-N` identifier (`GT-N?` when the ground truth is unverified) or a `Cn` identifier, optionally followed by a parenthesized gloss, joined to the next by `+`. The mechanical form check detects that violation only when the prose input is the last one before the first `→`; in an earlier position the check matches the well-formed remainder and scores the head conforming, so the rule binds in positions the check does not reach.

351	### Converting structured-technique outputs into chains
352	
353	Structured-technique outputs (trade-off matrices, second-order effect lists) do not appear in this section as-is — each converts into the chain format above using the rule for its technique below. This subsection is the single source of truth for the conversion; the per-technique Handoff sections point back here rather than restating it, so future structured techniques extend this one place.
354	
355	**Trade-off matrix → one chain.** A trade-off matrix collapses into ONE chain whose intermediate cites the winning weighted total and whose endpoint names a single recommended option:
356	
357	```text
358	GT-refs (criteria's factual basis) → weighted totals (the winning total vs. the runner-up, naming the high-weight criteria that drive it) → recommended option
359	```
360	
361	Example: `GT-2 + GT-5 (criteria facts) → weighted totals: B=82 > A=64, driven by reliability×warranty → recommend B`. The full matrix stays in the technique's own output — this subsection carries only the single collapsed chain, never the matrix re-expressed row-by-row (that would violate the one-chain-per-conclusion rule above). An exact tie between weighted totals still resolves to a single named recommended option; a tie must not produce a multi-option chain endpoint. **Exact-tie tiebreak (deterministic):** on an exact tie, prefer the option with fewer `GT-N?` (unverified) inputs among its winning criteria; if still tied, name both totals in the chain intermediate but select the first-listed option as the chain endpoint, and flag the tie explicitly in the Conclusion section's confidence line.
362	
363	**Second-order effect list → order-marked extension.** A second-order effect list extends the parent chain IN PLACE as additional order-marked steps, each carrying the same evidentiary discipline as the first-order steps that produced the conclusion:
364	
365	```text
366	GT-N → first-order conclusion →[2nd] [2nd-order effect] →[3rd] [3rd-order effect] (contradicts GT-M → back to Phase 2)
367	```
368	
369	Example: `GT-1 → first-order conclusion →[2nd] flag-config surface grows →[3rd] flag debt accumulates (contradicts GT-4 → back to P2)`. The order marks (`[2nd]`, `[3rd]`) make the extension's sequence legible. A contradicting effect routes the conclusion back to Phase 2 — never directly to Phase 3 or past Phase 2. A pass that surfaces no non-contradicting downstream effect leaves the parent chain unextended — a clean no-op, not an error.

371	### Confidence levels, defined
372	
373	`HIGH`, `MEDIUM` and `LOW` name how much of a chain is **outstanding** — not how strongly the analysis believes its conclusion. Three axes decide the band, each answerable by inspecting what the chain already carries on the page:
374	
375	- **Inputs** — the provenance of every identifier on the head line: an unsuffixed `GT-N` with a named read-at-source location, a `?`-marked ground truth, or a `Cn` carrying its own band.
376	- **Inference** — whether each hop the chain's endpoint depends on follows from the line above it, or needs a premise supplied by an `[Assumes: A-N]` annotation.
377	- **Rivals** — whether a competing conclusion from the same ground truths survives, and what rules it out. Section 5 is where the ruling-out is written down, so a chain answers this axis by pointing at its own Abandoned Reasoning entry as readily as by carrying the rival on its confidence line.
378	
379	**The band is the lowest the three axes license.** A chain is not HIGH because two of them are clean.
380	
381	**HIGH — nothing on this chain is outstanding.** Every identifier on the head line is an unsuffixed `GT-N` whose read-at-source location is named, or a `Cn` itself rated HIGH; every hop the endpoint depends on follows from the line above it by deduction, by arithmetic that recomputes when redone independently of the chain text, or by a regularity cited to an unsuffixed ground truth; and the strongest rival conclusion the analysis considered is named — on this confidence line or in a section 5 entry this chain points to — together with the ground truth or chain that rules it out, that ruling-out input itself unsuffixed. A chain whose endpoint a live alternative still contests is unexamined, not certain: it is MEDIUM at best.
382	
383	An `[Assumes: A-N]` annotation on a hop shorts the Inference axis **unless** the confidence line says what becomes of the endpoint when that assumption fails and the endpoint still stands — *"A2 is that the CDN'd assets are versioned; if they were not, the CDN result would be weaker evidence still, so the conclusion is unaffected"*. An annotation on a hop that only qualifies a second-order extension, and not the endpoint, is outside this axis and the chain says which case it is. Stating the sensitivity is the work; an unexamined assumption is not the same thing as one whose falsity has been priced.
384	
385	The Rivals axis is answered when a section 5 entry names a competing conclusion to this chain's endpoint and the chain or ground truth that ruled it out, or when the endpoint is itself a ruling-out — a chain establishing that some option does not work has already done the rival's work and does not need a rival of its own. It is short when a competing conclusion has been raised anywhere in the analysis and nothing settles it, and when the analysis reaches a positive recommendation with no section 5 content bearing on it at all.
386	
387	**MEDIUM — exactly one axis is short, and the shortfall is named and bounded.** One of: an identifier on the head line is `?`-marked or is a `Cn` rated MEDIUM; or at most one hop the endpoint depends on rests on a stated `[Assumes: A-N]` premise whose failure the chain has not priced; or a rival to the endpoint is live and nothing in the analysis settles it. The confidence line names which axis is short, names the specific input, hop or rival, and states what would close it — the verification that would remove an input as a cause of the downgrade, the evidence that would establish an assumed premise, or the observation that would settle between this conclusion and its rival. A MEDIUM chain is one whose weakness a reader can point at.
388	
389	**LOW — the shortfall is unbounded, or more than one axis is short.** Two or more axes short at once; or an input is `?` with no verification path available; or a hop's missing premise cannot be stated as an assumption at all, so the analysis cannot say what would make the step valid; or a rival survives that no available observation would settle. A LOW chain is reportable, and a conclusion resting on it alone is not actionable.
390	
391	**Calibration rule.** Each rating is the highest its inputs, hops and rivals license, **and no higher**. Rating above what the axes license over-claims. Rating below it is a defect of the same kind: a chain meeting HIGH on all three axes and written MEDIUM misreports the analysis's own strength, and a document whose every chain carries the same defensive band tells a reader nothing about which parts to trust. Criterion 5 scores calibration, not altitude — an analysis whose every band is the one its axes license is Rigorous whether its conclusion is HIGH, MEDIUM or LOW.
392	
393	**The caps are consequences, not extra rules.** The unverified-input rule (D-07) below and the ceiling at the lowest-rated chain a head cites are what the Inputs axis says, restated for the two cases that occur most often; they are the fast check, and these definitions are what they check for. A cap never licenses a band on its own — it bounds from above, and the band is still the lowest any of the three axes licenses.
394	
395	**Confidence pre-check (Inputs axis).** Directly above every `**Confidence:**` line — each §4 chain's and the §6 Conclusion's — write one `**Pre-check:**` line, with nothing between it and the `**Confidence:**` line it checks:
396	
397	```text
398	**Pre-check:** head GT-1, GT-3?, C2 (MEDIUM) · ?-marked: GT-3? · lowest cited: MEDIUM · Inputs ceiling: MEDIUM
399	**Confidence:** MEDIUM — GT-3? is unverified; …
400	```
401	
402	Four fields, separated by ` · `: `head` lists every identifier on the chain's head line (the part before the first `→`), in order, comma-separated, a `?` suffix kept (`GT-3?`), each `Cn` followed by its own stated band in parentheses (`C2 (MEDIUM)`) — for the §6 roll-up, `head` is every chain the Conclusion rests on, each with its band, plus any `GT-N?` the Conclusion rests on directly. `?-marked` lists the `?`-suffixed identifiers from `head`, comma-separated, or the token `none`. `lowest cited` is the lowest band among the `Cn` in `head`, or `none` when `head` cites no chain. `Inputs ceiling` is the Inputs axis's bound: `LOW` if `lowest cited` is LOW; otherwise `MEDIUM` if `?-marked` is not `none` or `lowest cited` is MEDIUM; otherwise `HIGH`.
403	
404	This is the Inputs axis of "Confidence levels, defined" made procedural — Inference and Rivals are not scored on this line, and can only lower the band further. The ceiling bounds from above, as the caps-are-consequences paragraph above states; the `**Confidence:**` label may equal it or sit below it, and never above it — a below-ceiling label is explained by the Confidence line itself, not by the pre-check. In §6, the pre-check line is itself a Conclusion-section claim under the Claim inventory rule below, and it is cited by the chains its own `head` names.
405	
406	### Conclusion C1: [Conclusion text]
407	
408	GT-N ([brief fact label, source]) + GT-M ([brief fact label, source])
409	→ [intermediate claim — a new inference statable from combining GT-N and GT-M but from neither alone]
410	→ [conclusion — the claim this chain establishes]
411	
412	**Pre-check:** head [every head identifier; each Cn with its band, e.g. C2 (MEDIUM)] · ?-marked: [the GT-N? identifiers, or none] · lowest cited: [lowest Cn band, or none] · Inputs ceiling: [HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW]
413	**Confidence:** [HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW]
414	[If MEDIUM or LOW: name each GT-N? input with the verification that would remove it as a cause of the downgrade; name each Cn on this chain's head rated below HIGH, which need not be re-explained here; and give each downgrade cause belonging to this chain itself — for example a weak inference step or an absent-fails derivation — with what would remove it as a cause of the downgrade or a stated reason no verification path exists (the validation-rubric absent-fails EXCEPT clause, for an absent-fails derivation, or an explicit account of why no available evidence settles that cause).]
415	
416	**Unverified input rule (D-07):** A chain that includes any `GT-N?` input must end with a MEDIUM or LOW confidence line. The line must name the unverified input and state the verification that would remove it as a cause of the downgrade. A HIGH confidence claim cannot rest on an unverified ground truth. A chain is also rated no higher than the lowest-rated chain its head cites — the stated confidence label of each `Cn` on its head line, the part before the first `→`. This is a ceiling: it bounds the rating from above and is never a reason to rate a chain HIGH, and a cited chain rated MEDIUM under a validation-rubric EXCEPT clause still caps every chain that cites it. Every MEDIUM or LOW confidence line explains only its own chain's rating, so its validity never depends on how far away a cap originates. The line names each `GT-N?` input with the verification that would remove it as a cause of the downgrade. It names each `Cn` on the chain's head rated below HIGH and need not re-explain that `Cn`, whose own confidence line carries the explanation, so no line has to trace a cited chain's lineage. For each downgrade cause belonging to the chain itself — for example a weak inference step or an absent-fails derivation — the line states what would remove it as a cause of the downgrade or a stated reason no verification path exists. A stated reason is the validation-rubric absent-fails EXCEPT clause, for an absent-fails derivation, or an explicit account of why no available evidence settles that cause; "speculative" is never such a reason. The validation-rubric absent-fails EXCEPT clause is the only clause that can stand in for a verification path, and naming any other clause, including the speculative EXCEPT clause, stands in for nothing. A chain cited on another chain's head is load-bearing, so the rubric's speculative EXCEPT clause no longer covers it, and the cited chain's own confidence line states its verification path; a speculative chain with no verification path is not cited on another chain's head, and stays speculative or moves to Abandoned Reasoning (§5).
417	
418	---
419	
420	## 5. Abandoned Reasoning
421	
422	Record every reasoning path that was explored and discarded. This section is required in every analysis. Dead ends are not failures — they are part of the reasoning record and save future analysts from re-exploring paths that have already been ruled out.
423	
424	### Dead End: [Name of discarded path]
425	
426	**What was tried:** [Brief description of the reasoning path that was pursued.]
427	
428	**Why abandoned:** [The specific failure — assumption false, contradicts a ground truth, assumption classification too weak to anchor the chain, conclusion circular, intermediate could not be established, speculative with no verification path (so not cited on another chain's head), etc. Be precise: "we ran out of time" is not a valid abandonment reason.]
429	
430	**What it ruled out:** [What this dead end saves the reader from re-exploring. A well-documented dead end is as valuable as a live conclusion.]
431	
432	If no reasoning was abandoned, write:
433	
434	`Nothing material here — all reasoning paths pursued led to the conclusion above. [Optional: describe the problem's constraint space that made alternative paths infeasible.]`
435	
436	The escape valve still satisfies D-03. Do not omit the heading.
437	
438	---
439	
440	## 6. Conclusion
441	
442	Summarize the analysis result. The Conclusion section synthesizes what the Derivation Chains established — it does not introduce new claims or reasoning.
443	
444	**Recommended approach:** [Description of the recommended course of action, decision, or design choice.]
445	
446	**Key insight:** [The non-obvious finding the first-principles analysis revealed — what reasoning by analogy or convention would have missed.]
447	
448	**Trade-offs acknowledged:** [What is being accepted, deprioritized, or deferred as a result of this recommendation. No recommendation is free of trade-offs.]
449	
450	**Pre-check:** head [each chain the Conclusion rests on with its band, e.g. C1 (MEDIUM), C3 (HIGH); plus any GT-N? it rests on directly] · ?-marked: [ids, or none] · lowest cited: [lowest band, or none] · Inputs ceiling: [HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW]
451	**Confidence:** [HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW]
452	
453	If Confidence is MEDIUM or LOW: name each chain contributing to the Conclusion that is rated below HIGH, and each `GT-N?` input the Conclusion rests on directly with the verification that would remove it as a cause of the downgrade. The line need not restate a named chain's verification path or no-path reason; the named chain's own §4 confidence line carries it. Give any downgrade cause belonging to the Conclusion itself with what would remove it as a cause of the downgrade or a stated reason no verification path exists, as §4 defines. A MEDIUM or LOW conclusion without this explanation does not satisfy D-07.
454	
455	**Claim inventory.** A Conclusion-section claim is a bold lead-in whose colon closes the bold span, or a numbered or bulleted list item, and the four lead-ins this template prescribes — `**Recommended approach:**`, `**Key insight:**`, `**Trade-offs acknowledged:**` and `**Confidence:**` — are always claims and each must cite a chain; the `**Confidence:**` line discharges that obligation through the chains D-07 already requires it to name, and a HIGH line whose justification prose names no chain is the one position where this rule and the extractor can disagree, so name the chain there too; nothing inside a fenced block is ever a claim whatever its shape, a near-paraphrase restatement or direct entailment of an already-cited claim earlier in the same section is not a second claim, and prose carrying neither a bold colon lead-in nor a list marker is not a claim at all. Three bounds are measured, not assumed: a bold lead-in whose colon-terminated span is the entire physical line and carries no citation of its own is a section-intro label, and the citation obligation then falls to the list items beneath it; a bold span whose closing `**` is not immediately preceded by the colon is not matched at all — write `**Label:** text` to match, not `**Label: text**`; and a list item counts only when it closes its own sentence or runs past forty characters. Enumerate by this rule, not by recollection — the rule is the contract and the extractor is a partial instrument for it.
456	
457	**Citation form.** Every Conclusion-section claim either names the chain that established it inline — `(chain C1)` — or is discharged by a §6→§4 closure ledger row that quotes the claim and names its chain. A claim doing neither is cut, not softened. Ledger discharge requires the structural row form the closure-ledger example below shows — a list marker, then the quoted claim, then an arrow, then the chain id — and a prose sentence that merely quotes something and names a chain is not a ledger row. This is detected only when the row sits inside section 6: the ledger emitted as process output in the appendix after section 6 is not visible to the check, and inline citation is therefore the mechanically checkable form.
458	
459	**Conforming — inline chain citation:**
460	
461	```text
462	**Recommended approach:** Move sustained workloads to Fargate (chain C1).
463	```
464	
465	**Conforming — closure-ledger row:**
466	
467	```text
468	- "Move sustained workloads to Fargate" → chain C1 ✓
469	```
470	
471	**Non-conforming — a claim naming no chain and quoted by no ledger row:**
472	
473	```text
474	**Recommended approach:** Move sustained workloads to Fargate.
475	```
476	
477	Both forms are accepted because both discharge the same obligation: the ledger is process output emitted in the appendix after section 6 (see the agent body — `SKILL.md` on the skill surface, `agents/first-principles.md` on the agent surface — "Before presenting conclusions"), not a seventh output section, and the chain IDs cited are the `C1`/`C2` IDs assigned by §4's chain-numbering convention.
478	
479	**Caveats.** A caveat qualifying an existing Conclusion-section claim either names the chain it qualifies inline or carries the marker `no chain — flagged assumption only` (em dash, lower case, no trailing punctuation inside the marker), and a marked caveat still scores untraced: the marker discloses the gap, it does not discharge the claim, because it is honest labelling rather than a citation and the extractor is deliberately not taught to recognise it. A caveat doing neither is cut, not softened.
480	
481	**Not a claim — a bold lead-in alone on its line, carrying no citation:**
482	
483	```text
484	**Recommended approach — three steps, in this order:**
485	```
486	
487	This is the hinge of "detectable from the emission alone" — an author can dodge extraction by putting the lead-in on its own line, and the claim obligation then falls to the numbered items beneath it.
488	
489	**A claim — the same lead-in carrying its assertion on the same line:**
490	
491	```text
492	**Recommended approach:** Move sustained workloads to Fargate before evaluating Lambda (chain C1).
493	```
494	
495	Nothing follows the closing `**` in the block above and something does here, which is the whole difference.
496	
497	**A claim — the lead-in alone on its line, but carrying its own citation:**
498	
499	```text
500	**Recommended approach, established in chain C1:**
501	```
502	
503	The section-intro-label exclusion is conditional on carrying no citation; naming the chain inside the label keeps it a claim.
504	
505	**Not matched at all — a bold span whose colon sits inside it:**
506	
507	```text
508	**Overall confidence: HIGH.**
509	```
510	
511	The extractor requires the colon to close the bold span, so this line is not a claim and not a non-claim — it is never looked at.
512	
513	**A claim — the same statement with the colon closing the bold span:**
514	
515	```text
516	**Overall confidence:** HIGH — seven of eight chains rest on figures read at source (chain C1).
517	```
518	
519	One character moved, and the statement enters the inventory.
520	
521	**Not a claim — a short list item with no sentence-ending punctuation:**
522	
523	```text
524	- Measure duty cycle first
525	```
526	
527	Twenty-four characters and no terminal punctuation, so it falls under the assertiveness floor.
528	
529	**A claim — a short list item closing its own sentence:**
530	
531	```text
532	- Size the Savings Plan after cleanup.
533	```
534	
535	Also under forty characters, so the terminal punctuation is the only thing carrying it over the floor. The two items above are worded differently only so each block is uniquely locatable by the fixture-extraction guard — a true one-character minimal pair would make one block's text a literal prefix of the other's, which no substring needle can discriminate (the `R-HEAD-PERIOD-*` lesson) — and a later control proves the axis is punctuation by re-scoring each block with its punctuation toggled.
536	
537	**Conformant but still untraced — a caveat carrying the flagged-assumption marker:**
538	
539	```text
540	**Trade-offs acknowledged:** the ~73% figure is a ceiling requiring an all-upfront commitment; the realized figure on a no-upfront plan is materially lower — no chain — flagged assumption only.
541	```
542	
543	The marker satisfies the Caveats rule above and the claim still scores untraced; that is honesty-not-score, not a defect, and it is why the extractor is not taught to recognise the marker.
544	
545	**Conformant and traced — the same caveat citing the chain it qualifies:**
546	
547	```text
548	**Trade-offs acknowledged:** the ~73% figure is a ceiling requiring an all-upfront commitment; the realized figure on a no-upfront plan is materially lower (chain C5).
549	```
550	
551	Naming C5 discharges the claim; the marker discloses it. The two rewrites land on different Criterion 6 bands, and that band is assigned by a model — no gate in this tree checks it.

1	<!-- GENERATED — DO NOT EDIT. Source: shared/references/pre-mortem.md. Regenerate via: scripts/sync-content.py --write. -->
2	
3	# Pre-Mortem
4	
5	> A prospective-hindsight failure analysis tool. Reach for this when a proposed
6	> plan needs stress-testing before commitment — the goal is to surface probable
7	> failure causes before they materialise.
8	
9	---
10	
11	## When to reach for this
12	
13	Use a pre-mortem once a plan has enough specificity to reason about particular
14	failure modes, but before it is finalised and carries organizational momentum.
15	Not the right tool for evaluating options (use trade-off analysis) or for tracing
16	something that already went wrong (use 5-Whys).
17	
18	**Decision rule — pre-mortem vs. inversion:** pre-mortem stress-tests a **plan**;
19	[inversion](${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/references/inversion.md) stress-tests a **claim**. If a concrete plan with actions and a
20	timeline exists, pre-mortem is the right tool — it reasons about implementation failure
21	modes that claim-level inversion cannot see. With only a stated belief, conclusion, or
22	design principle in hand, inversion fits better. This is the same boundary
23	`inversion.md` states from its own side, and it is the one that matters most here:
24	Phase 5 selects between these two directly, so a reader arriving from that
25	prescription needs to know why they were sent here rather than there.
26	
27	---
28	
29	## Framing
30	
31	Before any other step, adopt this premise explicitly:
32	
33	> It is approximately six months from now. This plan has failed — not merely
34	> underperformed, but failed badly. That outcome is a fact.
35	> Working backward: what caused it?
36	
37	This past-tense framing is not rhetorical. It bypasses the optimism bias that
38	makes forward-looking risk lists generic. Do not skip it or soften it to
39	"might fail" — the grammatical shift from possibility to accomplished fact is
40	the mechanism.
41	
42	---
43	
44	## Procedure
45	
46	1. **Restate the premise.** Before writing anything, say or write: "The plan has
47	   already failed. What caused it?" This re-anchors the prospective-hindsight
48	   frame before analysis begins.
49	
50	2. **Write independently.** List every cause of the failure without filtering —
51	   write the full list before reviewing it. Do not discard causes that seem
52	   unlikely; the list is raw material, not a verdict. Generate from at least
53	   three named viewpoints — for example the implementer, the person who has to
54	   live with the result, whoever pays for it, and a competitor who benefits
55	   from the failure. One generator asked once returns one perspective's
56	   failures, and the causes it misses are systematically the ones outside the
57	   frame it was asked in.
58	
59	3. **Interrogate the list adversarially.** Re-read each item and ask which ones
60	   contradict the plan's own stated premise, or the recommendation the analysis
61	   is about to make. A cause that would embarrass the conclusion is higher
62	   signal than one that merely adds risk to it. In a facilitated session these
63	   are the items a junior participant suppresses; written by a single analyst
64	   they are the items that get hedged into vagueness rather than dropped, so
65	   look for the softened ones, not the missing ones.
66	
67	4. **Identify recurring patterns.** Look for failure causes that cluster — the
68	   same root (over-optimistic timeline, single point of dependency, assumption
69	   never validated). A cluster is a structural weakness in the plan, not an
70	   isolated risk.
71	
72	5. **Triage each cluster on two axes: plausibility and recoverability.** Not by
73	   a probability figure invented for the purpose — say which of these it is:
74	
75	   - **Fatal** — if it happens, the plan does not recover. These get a plan
76	     change, not a mitigation, however unlikely they seem.
77	   - **Costly but survivable** — the plan continues at a stated price. These get
78	     a mitigation and an owner.
79	   - **Tolerable** — record and move on.
80	
81	   Sort by recoverability *before* plausibility. A fatal-but-unlikely cause
82	   outranks a likely-but-tolerable one, and ranking by likelihood alone inverts
83	   exactly that comparison — which is the failure a pre-mortem exists to catch.
84	
85	6. **Give every fatal and costly cluster a tripwire.** A tripwire is the
86	   **observation that would tell you this failure is now underway**, named in
87	   advance: a threshold, a date, a signal, a metric crossing a line. "Watch
88	   integration risk" is not a tripwire; "the staging sync job fails twice in one
89	   week" is, and "we have not got a test environment by 14 March" is.
90	
91	   State who would see it and when they would look. A failure mode nobody is
92	   positioned to notice has no tripwire, and saying so plainly is more useful
93	   than writing one that will never fire. The pre-mortem's value is spent at the
94	   moment the list is written unless something converts a predicted failure into
95	   a detected one — that is what the tripwire is.
96	
97	7. **Act on findings.** Modify the plan to address the structural weaknesses, or
98	   explicitly accept the risk with a named mitigation. A pre-mortem with no
99	   downstream plan change was box-ticking.
100	
101	**Exit criterion:** The failure has been stated as having already happened, causes
102	are written from that stance, causes are clustered into structural weaknesses,
103	every cluster carries a triage verdict of fatal / costly but survivable /
104	tolerable, every fatal and costly cluster carries a tripwire with an owner or an
105	explicit statement that no observable one exists, and every cluster has either a
106	named plan change or an explicitly accepted risk with a named mitigation. A
107	pre-mortem that ends without one of those two outcomes per cluster is
108	box-ticking, not a finding.
109	
110	---
111	
112	## Output contract
113	
114	The exit criterion above names four things the pre-mortem must produce. This is
115	what they look like on the page, in this order:
116	
117	**Premise** — one line, past tense, stating the failure as accomplished fact.
118	Not "the plan might fail"; the grammatical shift is the mechanism, and a premise
119	written in the conditional has already lost it.
120	
121	**Causes** — the unfiltered list, one per line, written before any grouping
122	appears. The viewpoints from step 2 are visible in it: if every cause is a
123	technical one, step 2 was run once rather than three times. Writing the clusters
124	first and back-filling causes into them inverts the procedure and produces the
125	generic risk list the whole framing exists to avoid.
126	
127	**Clusters** — the structural weaknesses the causes fall into, each named, and
128	each naming the causes it absorbs. A cluster is a claim that several causes share
129	one root; a heading with one cause under it is a cause, not a cluster. When the
130	pre-mortem runs inside a first-principles analysis, each cluster also cites the
131	chain ids (`Cn`) or ground-truth ids (`GT-N`) it bears on, so the finding lands
132	somewhere a reader can check it against.
133	
134	**Disposition** — per cluster, one of exactly two things: a named plan change, or
135	an explicitly accepted risk with a named mitigation. "Worth watching", "we should
136	keep this in mind" and "a risk we accept" with nothing named after it are none of
137	the above. A cluster whose disposition is an accepted risk still names what makes
138	the risk survivable; that is what distinguishes accepting a risk from noticing one.
139	
140	A pre-mortem missing any of the four has not run. A pre-mortem whose causes list
141	is shorter than its cluster list ran backwards.
142	
143	---
144	
145	## Example
146	
147	**Plan:** Host a dinner party for twelve people in two weeks, cooking a full
148	three-course meal from scratch for the first time at this scale.
149	
150	**Framing applied:** It is two weeks from now. The dinner party has failed badly.
151	What caused it?
152	
153	**Backward-derived failure causes:**
154	- Underestimated preparation time; last two courses were served an hour late
155	- A key ingredient unavailable the day before; no substitution plan
156	- One course required equipment not owned and not sourced in advance
157	- Two guests had dietary restrictions not asked about until the day of
158	- Energy depleted by the time guests arrived; host unable to enjoy the evening
159	
160	**Pattern identified:** Every cause traces back to a single structural weakness —
161	no dry run at smaller scale and no contingency check before commitment. The plan
162	assumed novelty would resolve itself on the day.
163	
164	---
165	
166	## Failure modes
167	
168	**Forward-looking framing.** "What could go wrong?" produces a generic risk list.
169	If causes feel speculative and mild, the past-tense premise was not adopted.
170	
171	**Running it too early.** A pre-mortem on a plan with insufficient specificity
172	yields generic concerns. The plan must have enough detail to reason about
173	particular failure modes — vague plans produce vague analyses.
174	
175	**Anchoring (in group settings).** When facilitated, the most senior voice in the
176	room shapes the list. Run independent writing before any sharing — each
177	participant writes silently before the group compares lists.
178	
179	**First-speaker anchoring.** The first cause named draws subsequent thinking
180	toward it. Write exhaustively before ranking or grouping.
181	
182	**No follow-through.** A pre-mortem with no downstream plan change was
183	box-ticking. Findings must modify the plan or be explicitly accepted with
184	named mitigations.
185	
186	---
187	
188	## Handoff
189	
190	The probable failure causes identified here feed Phase 5 (Validate). Add the
191	highest-signal structural weaknesses to the adversarial validation pass — each
192	one is a weak-link candidate for the signed-off analysis to address or explicitly
193	accept.

3	# Self-Audit Gate
4	
5	> **Scope:** This is the Layer-3 scoring instrument read on demand by the validator-fix-repeat loop
6	> already resident in `SKILL.md`. It scores a completed first-principles analysis against the
7	> six-section output format defined in `references/output-template.md`. The loop instruction
8	> itself — when to apply, what to fix, when to stop — lives in `SKILL.md` under
9	> "Before presenting conclusions" and is **not** repeated here. Come here only to score
10	> an analysis in progress; use `SKILL.md` for the loop procedure and `output-template.md`
11	> for authoring guidance.
12	>
13	> **What this instrument scores:** the structure of *this analysis*. It is not a rubric for the
14	> subject matter. When a request asks for a rubric, scorecard, or grading scheme applied to the
15	> thing being analyzed — an article's argument, a proposal, a design — that is a **separate
16	> deliverable** that belongs in the analysis body. Producing it does not satisfy this gate, and
17	> this gate does not substitute for it. Both must appear. (Historically named the "Validation
18	> Rubric"; renamed because that name collided with subject-matter rubrics and the collision was
19	> observed to cause this gate to be skipped.)
20	
21	## How to Apply This Gate
22	
23	Score the completed analysis against all 6 criteria below. For each criterion, produce exactly
24	one verdict block in the format prescribed in the Verdict Block Format section. An analysis
25	clears this gate only when it satisfies **both** of the following conditions — clearing
26	one condition alone does not constitute a pass:
27	
28	1. **Gate cleared** — no criterion scores Absent.
29	2. **Hand-wavy cap cleared** — at most one criterion scores Hand-wavy.
30	
31	If either condition is not met, revise the analysis and re-score — bounded to **at most one re-perception pass** per analysis, per the rule stated in full under `SKILL.md`'s Turn discipline section. After that single pass, any criterion still failing — or newly failing as a result of the revision — is presented as an unresolved gap with a stated confidence caveat instead of being re-scored again.
32	
33	**Assumption Audit (verify before scoring)**
34	
35	The scan itself is not performed here — the agent already performed it at the end of Phase 4
36	(`SKILL.md`, "End-of-phase Assumption Audit") before this gate is ever applied. This
37	gate's job is narrower: verify the audit ran and its table is exhaustive, not repeat the
38	scan.
39	
40	Before scoring any criterion, confirm the audit table below is present in the analysis and
41	covers every named derivation chain step from section 4 — one row per chain per step, in
42	order, with no step skipped. Do not proceed to verdict blocks until this is confirmed. `Form conforming?` reads `unreached` where a rule binds at a position the mechanical check cannot reach — a disclosed gap in the check, never a softer `no`, and never to be scored as a conforming block. A row whose `Rule applied` cell explains that the check could not reach a position, while `Form conforming?` still reads `yes`, is scoring the block conforming on a rule it never checked; the verdict belongs in `Form conforming?`. `Band` is copied from the chain's own section-4 confidence label, so a disagreement between scan and chain is visible rather than reconciled silently. `Act attempted?` records whether the run tried to open a cited source for that chain's head inputs, and `Edges fired` which bounded re-entry edges fired for it. A load-bearing chain whose inputs are all `?`-marked and whose `Act attempted?` reads `no` is the shape this criterion most needs surfaced: a conclusion reached without once trying to check it.

120	## Scoring Model
121	
122	Score each of the 6 criteria using this shared 4-level scale, applied uniformly across all criteria
123	(highest to lowest):
124	
125	- **Rigorous** — the criterion's named artifact is present, structurally complete, and every
126	  entry meets the observable descriptor for this level: all required fields are populated with
127	  non-generic content, all required relationships are explicit,
128	  and every observable structural test in this criterion's Rigorous descriptor returns pass.
129	
130	- **Sound** — the criterion's named artifact is present and mostly meets the Rigorous descriptor,
131	  but one or more entries fall short in a specific, identifiable way: a field is generic or vague
132	  rather than empty, a relationship is implicit rather than absent, or one entry departs from the
133	  prescribed form without invalidating the rest.
134	
135	- **Hand-wavy** — the criterion's named artifact is present but fails the Rigorous descriptor in
136	  a pattern rather than an isolated entry: multiple fields are generic or empty, the artifact's
137	  prescribed structure is not followed, or the section uses the honest-depth escape valve with a
138	  reason that could be copy-pasted to any analysis without modification.
139	
140	- **Absent** — the criterion's named artifact is missing entirely, or the section exists but
141	  contains no content that could be scored against the artifact's descriptor (the section heading
142	  appears with nothing substantive below it).
143	
144	**Rank order (explicit):** Rigorous > Sound > Hand-wavy > Absent.
145	
146	**Gate:** Any criterion scored **Absent** fails the entire analysis — it must be revised and
147	re-scored, bounded to at most one re-perception pass per analysis, per "How to Apply This
148	Gate" above. If the criterion still scores Absent after that single pass, it is presented as
149	an unresolved gap with a stated confidence caveat instead of being withheld, regardless of how
150	all other criteria score.
151	
152	**Hand-wavy cap:** Two or more criteria scored **Hand-wavy** also fails the entire analysis —
153	the same bound applies: revise and re-score once, per "How to Apply This Gate" above. One
154	criterion at Hand-wavy is tolerated (one isolated weaker section does not indicate a systemic
155	quality problem); two or more at Hand-wavy indicates a pattern of shallow reasoning that the
156	gate alone cannot catch, because no single criterion has reached the gate-fail level. If two or
157	more criteria still score Hand-wavy after that single pass, the cap breach is presented as an
158	unresolved gap with a stated confidence caveat instead of being withheld.
159	
160	**Pass:** No criterion scores Absent, and at most one criterion scores Hand-wavy.
161	(Equivalently: every criterion is Sound or above, except at most one may be Hand-wavy.)
162	
163	**Escape-valve scoring (global rule, applies to every criterion):** Any section that
164	legitimately uses the honest-depth escape valve (`Nothing material here — [reason]`) is
165	scored **Rigorous** if the stated reason is specific to this analysis — it names a property
166	of this problem that makes the section's content unnecessary — and **Hand-wavy** if the
167	reason is generic or copy-pasteable to any analysis. A properly-used escape valve is
168	**never** scored Absent solely for using the escape valve: the per-criterion Absent
169	descriptors below apply to a section that is missing, empty, or filled with non-scoreable
170	content, not to a section that is honestly and specifically marked as having no material
171	content.
172	
173	**Load-bearing chain (definition):** A derivation chain is *load-bearing* if a claim in
174	the Conclusion section (output section 6) depends on it — i.e., the chain produces, or is
175	cited as support for, a conclusion the analysis actually presents. A chain that reaches
176	only an intermediate result no conclusion rests on is not load-bearing. (This is the
177	narrower scoring sense of the phrase `SKILL.md` uses informally as "load-bearing for a
178	high-stakes conclusion.")

406	  premises on hops the endpoint does not depend on; a hop citing
407	  a regularity to a `GT-N?` ground truth is an Inputs-axis matter Criterion 3/5 scores, not a
408	  failure to follow.
409	
410	- **Sound** — chains exist for all conclusions, but one or more chains lack a genuine
411	  intermediate step (the chain goes directly from its head inputs to conclusion, or the stated
412	  intermediate is a restatement of one of its named inputs rather than a new inference); OR
413	  a conclusion has more than one derivation chain — redundant restatement rather than a
414	  missing chain — where the prescribed form is exactly one chain per conclusion; OR
415	  one dead end in Abandoned Reasoning is described with a vague abandonment reason
416	  ("seemed unlikely," "ran out of time") rather than the specific structural reason
417	  (assumption false, contradicts a GT, circular, intermediate could not be established); OR
418	  one or more chains render their hops as an ordered list (`1.`, `2.`, `3.`) instead of the
419	  prescribed arrow-led hop form, OR break a single hop across physical lines rather than
420	  splitting it into two hops, which splits one chain into disconnected
421	  fragments even where every hop is individually sound; OR a hop fails to follow, or its
422	  arithmetic does not recompute, where the endpoint does not depend on that hop; OR a hop the
423	  endpoint depends on carries an arithmetic error that leaves the endpoint unchanged — the
424	  only case of a hop the endpoint depends on that this band admits, and it covers arithmetic
425	  only: a hop the endpoint depends on that does not follow by deduction or cited regularity is
426	  Hand-wavy, whatever the grader judges its effect on the endpoint — **this clause is why the criterion
427	  cannot be scored on reasoning quality alone.** A chain that names its inputs, carries a
428	  genuine intermediate and reaches a conclusion satisfies every other Rigorous requirement
429	  while still failing the prescribed form; scoring only the semantics is what lets a
430	  Rigorous verdict coexist with a section of malformed chains.
431	
432	- **Hand-wavy** — some conclusions lack derivation chains; OR chains reference GT-IDs that
433	  do not appear in the Ground Truths section; OR an analogy is used as direct evidence
434	  ("others have solved it this way," "industry standard is X") without grounding in a named
435	  GT about that other situation; OR the Abandoned Reasoning section uses the honest-depth
436	  escape valve with a reason that is generic and would apply equally to any analysis (e.g.,
437	  "no dead ends were encountered," "all reasoning paths worked"); OR a hop the endpoint
438	  depends on does not follow by deduction or cited regularity (a non-sequitur) — including
439	  a hop whose only gap is an undeclared premise — or an arithmetic error changes the endpoint; an arithmetic error that leaves the endpoint unchanged
440	  is the Sound clause above, not this one — **this clause is why the criterion cannot be scored
441	  on form alone either.** A chain can name
442	  its inputs, carry a genuine intermediate, render every hop in the prescribed form and reach
443	  a conclusion while a hop the endpoint depends on does not follow.
444	
445	- **Absent** — no derivation chains exist in the document; OR the Derivation Chains section
446	  is absent or empty; OR conclusions appear in section 6 with no corresponding chains in
447	  section 4 — the core question's answer cannot be traced to any named ground truth.
448	
449	### Criterion 5: Validate
450	
451	Scores the **signed-off analysis** — the complete output with all conclusions traced and weak
452	links resolved or explicitly flagged with confidence caveats — across all six output sections,
453	focusing on the confidence caveats attached to the Derivation Chains (output section 4).
454	
455	- **Rigorous** — every derivation chain's weakest link is named; every MEDIUM or LOW confidence
456	  caveat, on a chain or on the Conclusion section, explains only its own rating: it names each
457	  GT-N? input it rests on directly, with the verification that would remove that input as a
458	  cause of the downgrade, and each Cn its head cites — or, for the Conclusion section, each
459	  contributing chain — that is rated below HIGH, and it need not re-explain a named Cn, whose
460	  own caveat carries its explanation; and for each downgrade cause belonging to the chain or
461	  Conclusion itself, such as a weak inference step or an absent-fails derivation, it states
462	  what would remove it as a cause of the downgrade or a stated reason no verification path
463	  exists, that reason being either, for an absent-fails derivation, the absent-fails EXCEPT
464	  clause below, the only clause that can stand in for a verification path, or an explicit
465	  account of why no available evidence settles that cause;
466	  the overall Conclusion section's confidence rating (HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW) matches the weakest
467	  chain that contributes to it, counting only chains not covered by an EXCEPT clause stated in
468	  this same descriptor; no chain that consumes a GT-N? input is rated HIGH confidence; every
469	  chain is rated no higher than the lowest-rated chain its head cites, a ceiling that holds
470	  even when a cited chain is rated MEDIUM under an EXCEPT clause below.
471	  Every rating is calibrated: each chain carries the band its inputs, hops and rivals
472	  license under the three-axis definition in `output-template.md` — no chain rated above
473	  what those axes permit, and none rated below it. A Conclusion claim supported by
474	  at least one HIGH-confidence chain may be presented at HIGH; a claim with no such
475	  chain is presented at the band its weakest contributing chain licenses, and presenting
476	  it so is Rigorous rather than a shortfall. Under-rating is a defect of the same kind
477	  as over-rating, and this criterion scores calibration, not altitude. EXCEPT: a chain is explicitly marked speculative — for
478	  example `[Speculative]` — and the analysis states, in the same place, that the claim it
479	  supports is not load-bearing and is offered for exploration only; that mark plus that
480	  statement is the satisfying evidence, and the chain may remain MEDIUM, though its confidence
481	  line still gives each of its own downgrade causes what would remove it or an explicit account
482	  of why no available evidence settles it, because the mark is not a no-path reason; a
483	  speculative chain cited on another chain's head is load-bearing and no longer satisfies this
484	  EXCEPT clause, so a speculative chain with no verification path is not cited on another
485	  chain's head and instead stays speculative or moves to Abandoned Reasoning (output section 5).
486	  EXCEPT: a chain is
487	  an absent-fails derivation — of the form "if [assumption] were true we could conclude X;
488	  [assumption] is false; therefore X does not follow" — whose named false assumption is the
489	  satisfying evidence, and the chain may remain MEDIUM because it establishes what does not
490	  follow rather than what does.
491	
492	  The adversarial pass Phase 5 prescribes has run and its record is complete: each computed
493	  figure's recompute, the sensitivity ground truth and whether it is `?`-marked, the rival and
494	  where it is ruled out or carried live, a premise stated in the past tense, an unfiltered
495	  cause list written before any grouping, clusters each naming the chain ids or ground-truth
496	  ids the weakness bears on, per cluster a named plan change or an explicitly accepted risk
497	  with a named mitigation, and the falsification condition — each part present or carrying its
498	  step's not-applicable line. Each structural weakness the pass
499	  returned has landed somewhere a reader can find it — as a named weak link on a chain, or as
500	  an explicit confidence caveat on the conclusion it threatens. An analysis whose conclusion is
501	  neither a plan nor a claim satisfies the Premise, Causes, Clusters and Disposition parts by
502	  carrying the `adversarial pass not applicable — [reason]` line with its reason named — that
503	  line is the adversarial-technique step's own not-applicable line, not a waiver of the whole
504	  record, so the Recompute, Sensitivity, Rival and Falsification parts each still carry their
505	  content or their own step's not-applicable line; an analysis that does carry a plan or a claim
506	  cannot satisfy the technique step that way, and the reason given is what makes the two cases
507	  distinguishable.
508	
509	  **A conclusion without a HIGH chain is not a shortfall.** A conclusion resting on no
510	  HIGH-confidence chain, uncovered by either EXCEPT clause above, is Rigorous on this
511	  criterion when every band it rests on is the band that chain's axes license and the
512	  Conclusion's own rating equals its weakest contributing chain's. A MEDIUM or LOW overall
513	  Conclusion rating remains a legitimate, honestly-caveated analysis — `output-template.md`
514	  permits it and this criterion now scores it Rigorous when it is calibrated. What bands
515	  this criterion below Rigorous is a band that does not match its axes in either direction,
516	  never a band that is merely low, and a verdict block reporting Rigorous alongside a
517	  MEDIUM overall rating is the expected shape of an honest analysis rather than a
518	  contradiction. An exception is claimed, not assumed: an analysis relying on one of the
519	  two EXCEPT clauses above names it in the Criterion 5 verdict block and cites the evidence
520	  that clause requires; an unclaimed exception is not applied on the analysis's behalf.
521	
522	- **Sound** — confidence ratings exist on chains, but a MEDIUM or LOW confidence line omits a
523	  GT-N? input it rests on directly, or a Cn its head cites (or, on the Conclusion section, a
524	  contributing chain) that is rated below HIGH, or a downgrade cause belonging to its own chain
525	  or Conclusion — including a MEDIUM or LOW rating that no named GT-N? input or Cn accounts for
526	  and whose line names no cause of its own; OR a confidence line names a GT-N? input without the
527	  verification that would remove it as a cause of the downgrade; OR a confidence line gives a
528	  downgrade cause belonging to its own chain or Conclusion with neither what would remove it as
529	  a cause of the downgrade nor a permitted no-path reason — for an absent-fails derivation, the
530	  absent-fails EXCEPT clause, or an explicit account of why no available evidence settles that
531	  cause — including a line whose only account of such a cause is the speculative EXCEPT clause
532	  or any clause other than the absent-fails one; OR a chain's head cites a chain marked
533	  speculative that has no verification path; OR a chain is rated HIGH confidence while consuming
534	  a GT-N? input (the rating does not match the unverified-input rule); OR a chain is rated above
535	  the lowest-rated chain its head cites; OR a single chain's band does not match what its
536	  three axes license, in either direction — a chain rated HIGH whose head carries a `?` or
537	  whose hops rest on a stated `[Assumes: A-N]` premise, or a chain meeting all three axes
538	  rated MEDIUM — while every other chain in the analysis is correctly banded; OR an
539	  adversarial pass record, or the `adversarial pass not applicable — [reason]` line, is present
540	  but one or more of the Recompute, Sensitivity, Rival and Falsification parts is absent and
541	  carries no not-applicable line of its own — a step silently omitted from a pass that otherwise
542	  ran.
543	
544	- **Hand-wavy** — confidence ratings appear on the overall Conclusion section but are absent
545	  from individual derivation chains; OR weak links are described in general terms ("some
546	  assumptions remain uncertain") without naming the specific chain step or GT-N? input that
547	  caused the concern; OR an adversarial pass record is present but no cluster carries a
548	  disposition — neither a named plan change nor an explicitly accepted risk with a named
549	  mitigation — so the pass named structural weaknesses and acted on none of them; OR the record
550	  states its clusters without the cause list they were drawn from, which is the generic risk
551	  list the pass exists to replace rather than a pass that produced one; OR two or more
552	  chains carry bands their axes do not license, so the miscalibration is a pattern rather
553	  than an isolated entry; OR every chain in the analysis carries the same band and no
554	  confidence line names which axis produced it, which is a default setting rather than a
555	  rating.
556	
557	- **Absent** — no confidence ratings appear anywhere in the derivation chains; OR GT-N? inputs
558	  are used in load-bearing chains without any confidence caveat anywhere in the document; OR
559	  — covering the case the first two clauses miss — confidence ratings exist but no weak-link
560	  identification or chain inspection was performed at all, so there is no evidence that
561	  Phase 5's stress-test operation was executed; OR neither an adversarial pass record nor an
562	  `adversarial pass not applicable — [reason]` line appears anywhere in the response, so there
563	  is no evidence that Phase 5's adversarial pass was executed at all. These two clauses are
564	  separate readings: a weakest-link paragraph written by the same reasoning that built the
565	  chains satisfies the first and not the second, and an analysis scoring above Absent on the
566	  strength of that paragraph alone is what this clause exists to catch.
567	
568	### Criterion 6: Conclusion-to-Ground-Truth Traceability
569	
570	Scores the relationship between the **Conclusion section** (section 6) claims and the
571	**Derivation Chains** (section 4) that produced them — a cross-section structural property
572	of the signed-off analysis as a whole. Quoted span: where the band is determined by whether a section-6 claim traces to a named section-4 chain, it must be drawn from the self-audit scan's claim-inventory table row or rows that determine the band, not from the Conclusion prose directly. Where the band is determined by the Key Insight being a restatement of the recommended approach rather than a non-obvious finding — a semantic property the claim-inventory table carries no column for — quote the analysis text directly.
573	
574	- **Rigorous** — every claim in the Conclusion section (recommended approach, key insight,
575	  trade-offs acknowledged) traces to a specific named derivation chain in section 4; the
576	  Conclusion section introduces no new claims that did not appear in section 4; the Key
577	  Insight names a non-obvious finding — a result that reasoning by analogy or convention
578	  does not reach — rather than restating the recommended approach.
579	
580	- **Sound** — most Conclusion claims trace to chains in section 4, but one claim is introduced
581	  for the first time in the Conclusion section (new reasoning not present in any derivation
582	  chain); OR the Key Insight is a restatement of the recommended approach rather than a
583	  non-obvious finding.
584	
585	- **Hand-wavy** — the Conclusion section contains claims that contradict or are inconsistent
586	  with the derivation chains in section 4; OR multiple new claims appear in the Conclusion
587	  section that are not present in any derivation chain.
588	
589	- **Absent** — the Conclusion section contains claims with no corresponding derivation chain
590	  anywhere in section 4; OR the Conclusion section is absent or empty; OR every item in the
591	  Conclusion is new reasoning not established by any derivation chain — the Conclusion section
592	  has been used to introduce the analysis's conclusions rather than to synthesize them.
593	
594	The extraction and caveat rules the bands above are scored against are stated here verbatim so the grading instrument carries them, not just the surface it grades.
595	
596	A Conclusion-section claim is a bold lead-in whose colon closes the bold span, or a numbered or bulleted list item, and the four lead-ins this template prescribes — `**Recommended approach:**`, `**Key insight:**`, `**Trade-offs acknowledged:**` and `**Confidence:**` — are always claims and each must cite a chain; the `**Confidence:**` line discharges that obligation through the chains D-07 already requires it to name, and a HIGH line whose justification prose names no chain is the one position where this rule and the extractor can disagree, so name the chain there too; nothing inside a fenced block is ever a claim whatever its shape, a near-paraphrase restatement or direct entailment of an already-cited claim earlier in the same section is not a second claim, and prose carrying neither a bold colon lead-in nor a list marker is not a claim at all. Three bounds are measured, not assumed: a bold lead-in whose colon-terminated span is the entire physical line and carries no citation of its own is a section-intro label, and the citation obligation then falls to the list items beneath it; a bold span whose closing `**` is not immediately preceded by the colon is not matched at all — write `**Label:** text` to match, not `**Label: text**`; and a list item counts only when it closes its own sentence or runs past forty characters. Enumerate by this rule, not by recollection — the rule is the contract and the extractor is a partial instrument for it.
597	
598	A caveat qualifying an existing Conclusion-section claim either names the chain it qualifies inline or carries the marker `no chain — flagged assumption only` (em dash, lower case, no trailing punctuation inside the marker), and a marked caveat still scores untraced: the marker discloses the gap, it does not discharge the claim, because it is honest labelling rather than a citation and the extractor is deliberately not taught to recognise it. A caveat doing neither is cut, not softened.
599	
600	---
601	
602	## Usage Note
603	
604	Score every criterion. Produce one verdict block per criterion, using the prescribed format
605	from the Verdict Block Format section above. The analysis must clear the gate (no criterion
606	at Absent) and the hand-wavy cap (at most one criterion at Hand-wavy) before conclusions are
607	presented. If either condition is not met, revise the relevant sections and re-score — bounded
608	to **at most one re-perception pass** per analysis, per the rule stated in full under "How to
609	Apply This Gate" at the top of this document. If a criterion still fails after that single
610	pass, present it as an unresolved gap with a stated confidence caveat instead of re-scoring
611	again. This closing note restates that bound; it does not create a second, looser one.

2	
3	# Trade-Off Analysis
4	
5	> Structures a choice between two or more genuinely viable options by weighting
6	> criteria before scoring — preventing the reverse-engineering of weights to
7	> justify a decision already made intuitively.
8	
9	---
10	
11	## When to reach for this
12	
13	Use this tool when two or more options are viable (none obviously dominant), the
14	choice spans multiple criteria that pull in different directions, and an
15	intuitive pick would be hard to justify to others.
16	
17	Do not use it when one option dominates on every relevant criterion — that is a
18	direct decision, not a trade-off.
19	
20	---
21	
22	## Procedure
23	
24	1. **Name the options — including the status quo.** List each option being
25	   compared, and **always include doing nothing** as one of them, named as what
26	   it concretely is ("keep the current 70/30 split", "stay on REST/JSON"). A
27	   comparison whose option set is all-change silently assumes change is
28	   warranted and reports that assumption back as a finding. If the status quo is
29	   genuinely unavailable — a contract expires, the hardware is failing — say so
30	   in one line and list it as ruled out; do not omit it silently. **Include a
31	   composite too:** when the named options can be split or combined — part of
32	   one and part of another, or one now and another later — list at least one
33	   such composite as its own option. A comparison limited to the options as the
34	   question named them cannot find that a mix of them is best. If the options
35	   genuinely cannot combine, say why in one line and list the composite as ruled
36	   out; do not omit it silently.
37	
38	2. **State the must-haves and apply them as knock-outs.** Before any scoring,
39	   name the conditions an option must satisfy to be viable at all. An option
40	   that fails a must-have is **eliminated, not scored low** — report it under
41	   `## Options` as knocked out, with the must-have it failed. Scoring a
42	   non-viable option lets a high weighted total out-vote a hard constraint,
43	   which is how an option that cannot actually be chosen wins a trade-off.
44	   If nothing is a must-have, write "no must-haves" rather than skipping the
45	   step — the two are different claims.
46	
47	3. **List criteria.** Identify 5–8 criteria that matter to this decision. Lock
48	   this list — add no new criteria after this step. If a criterion matters, it
49	   must appear now.
50	
51	4. **Assign weights. Lock them now.** Give each criterion a relative weight
52	   (1–5) before scoring any option. If you cannot assign weights without first
53	   seeing how options score, stop — locking weights before scoring is the core
54	   discipline that prevents reverse-engineering them to favor an intuitive pick.
55	
56	5. **Anchor the scale, then score.** Before scoring, state for each criterion
57	   what a **1** and a **5** concretely mean — the anchors. "Cost: 1 = over
58	   $20k, 5 = under $2k" is an anchor; "Cost: 1 = bad, 5 = good" is not. Then
59	   score each option on each criterion independently (1–5) against those
60	   anchors. Phrase every criterion so higher is always better (e.g.,
61	   "Reliability" not "Reliability risk") — a mixed scale silently inverts the
62	   result. Without anchors a score means only "how I felt about this option",
63	   and the arithmetic that follows inherits that and dresses it as a number.
64	
65	6. **Cite the ground truth each score rests on.** Every score names the
66	   `GT-ID`s that justify it. A score resting on a `GT-N?` input carries that
67	   `?` forward: per D-07, the chain this trade-off collapses into is capped at
68	   **MEDIUM** and its confidence line names the unverified input and the
69	   verification that would remove it. A score with no ground truth behind it is
70	   a preference — mark it as one rather than citing nothing.
71	
72	7. **Compute:** multiply weight × score per criterion; sum per option.
73	
74	8. **Read the result.** The highest weighted total among the surviving options
75	   is the recommendation. If it surprises you, only re-examine a weight when you
76	   can state why it was wrong *before* seeing the result — adjusting weights
77	   afterward is the failure mode this procedure prevents.
78	
79	**Flip test — run it every time, not only on a near-tie.** Report the
80	**smallest weight change that changes the winner**: name the criterion, the
81	weight it would have to move to, and how far that is from the weight you
82	locked. Then ask whether that weight is genuinely wrong. A winner that survives
83	only a ±1 move on one criterion is a near-tie whatever the totals look like,
84	and a winner that survives every single-criterion move is a robust result —
85	both are findings, and neither is visible from the totals alone. Report the
86	flip distance under `## Recommendation`. Do not refine scores to break a
87	near-tie; refining manufactures false precision. If no single-criterion change
88	flips the result, say that explicitly — "no single weight change flips this"
89	is the strongest result this procedure can return, and it is worth stating.
90	
91	---
92	
93	## Example
94	
95	**Decision:** Laptop for a parent who browses, video-calls, and writes
96	documents.
97	
98	**Ground truths this rests on:**
99	
100	- **GT-1** — the current machine drops video calls roughly weekly (observed over
101	  two months).
102	- **GT-2** — refurbished units from this vendor carry a 90-day warranty; new
103	  units carry 12 months (vendor's published terms, read at source).
104	- **GT-3?** — refurbished failure rates are "around twice" new in the first
105	  year. *Unverified — recalled from a review article, source not located.*
106	
107	**Step 1 — options named, status quo included:**
108	
109	- **A** — refurbished mid-range
110	- **B** — new entry-level
111	- **C** — keep the current laptop (status quo)
112	
113	**Step 2 — must-haves applied as knock-outs:**
114	
115	| Must-have | A | B | C |
116	|---|---|---|---|
117	| Holds a video call without dropping | ✓ | ✓ | **✗ (GT-1)** |
118	
119	**C is knocked out, not scored.** Had it been scored instead, its perfect cost
120	score (5 × 3 = 15, nothing to spend) would have carried it close to A on a
121	total — while still failing the one thing the machine is being replaced *for*.
122	This is the failure mode step 2 exists to prevent.
123	
124	**Steps 3-4 — criteria and weights locked before any scoring:**
125	
126	| Criterion                       | Weight | 1 means…                    | 5 means…                     |
127	|----------------------------------|--------|-----------------------------|------------------------------|
128	| Performance                      | 4      | stutters on a video call    | headroom for years           |
129	| Reliability                      | 5      | failure expected in year 1  | failure unlikely in 5 years  |
130	| Cost                             | 3      | over $900                   | under $300                   |
131	| Warranty / support               | 4      | none                        | 12 months or more            |
132	| Portability                      | 2      | desk-bound                  | carried daily without thought|
133	| Ease of setup (non-technical)    | 3      | needs a technical helper    | works out of the box         |
134	
135	**Step 5-7 — scored against those anchors, with the ground truth behind each:**
136	
137	| Option     | Performance (×4) | Reliability (×5) | Cost (×3)  | Warranty (×4) | Portability (×2) | Ease of setup (×3) | Total  |
138	|------------|------------------|------------------|------------|---------------|------------------|--------------------|--------|
139	| A (refurb) | 4 × 4 = 16       | 2 × 5 = 10       | 5 × 3 = 15 | 2 × 4 = 8     | 3 × 2 = 6        | 3 × 3 = 9          | **64** |
140	| B (new)    | 2 × 4 = 8        | 5 × 5 = 25       | 3 × 3 = 9  | 5 × 4 = 20    | 4 × 2 = 8        | 4 × 3 = 12         | **82** |
141	
142	Reliability scores rest on **GT-3?**; warranty scores on **GT-2**.
143	
144	**Step 8 — result:** B scores 82 vs. A's 64, a gap of 18, driven by reliability
145	and warranty.
146	
147	**Flip test:** no single weight change within the 1–5 scale flips this result.
148	The closest is Reliability 5 → 1, which closes the gap from 18 to 6 — and that
149	move means asserting reliability barely matters for a machine bought *because*
150	the current one fails. Every other single-criterion move leaves a wider gap
151	(Warranty 4 → 1 leaves 9; Cost 3 → 5 leaves 14). The recommendation is robust
152	in the sense this test can establish.
153	
154	**Confidence:** MEDIUM, not HIGH. Reliability carries the heaviest weight (5)
155	and its scores rest on **GT-3?**, which is unverified — so per D-07 the chain
156	this collapses into is capped at MEDIUM. Locating a failure-rate figure in the
157	vendor's own return data, or a cited reliability study, would remove that cause.
158	Note what the flip test does *not* do here: it varies weights, not scores, so a
159	robust flip result does not repair an unverified input.
160	
161	---
162	
163	## Failure modes
164	
165	- **Weights set after scoring.** If you scored options before assigning
166	  weights, the weights will unconsciously reflect the scores — discard and
167	  restart from step 4.
168	
169	- **Too many criteria.** More than 8 criteria dilute the signal toward noise —
170	  prune to those that genuinely differentiate the options.
171	
172	- **Criteria added mid-analysis.** Adding a criterion after seeing partial
173	  scores is almost always rationalizing — lock the list at step 3 and restart.
174	
175	- **Treating a near-tie as a precision problem.** Refining scores to break a
176	  near-tie manufactures false precision; run the flip test instead.
177	
178	- **Criteria that are not independent.** Two criteria measuring the same factor
179	  (e.g., "cost" and "budget impact") double-count it — merge or drop one.
180	
181	- **The status quo left off the option list.** An all-change option set assumes
182	  change is warranted and then reports that assumption as a finding. Doing
183	  nothing is an option until a stated must-have rules it out (step 1).
184	
185	- **A must-have scored instead of applied.** Scoring a non-viable option lets a
186	  high weighted total out-vote a hard constraint, so an option that cannot
187	  actually be chosen can win. Knock it out at step 2 and say which must-have it
188	  failed.
189	
190	- **Unanchored scores.** Without stated 1-and-5 anchors a score records how the
191	  option felt, and the arithmetic launders that into a number. Anchors are what
192	  make two options comparable — and the same analysis reproducible.
193	
194	- **The flip test skipped because the totals look decisive.** A wide gap can
195	  still rest on one weight. Run the test every time; "no single weight change
196	  flips this" is a real and reportable result, not a null one.
197	
198	- **A robust flip result read as confidence in the inputs.** The flip test
199	  varies *weights*, not scores. It says nothing about whether a `GT-N?` behind a
200	  score is true, and never lifts D-07's cap.
201

Here's how I'd think this through with you.

Start with the number everyone fixates on: the $70K. It's real, but it's not $70K. Oregon's tax brackets are actually more compressed than California's — Oregon hits its top rate (9.9%) at just $125K of income, while California doesn't even reach 9.3% until way higher and doesn't hit double digits until $371K+. So contrary to the usual "California will eat your raise" assumption, the tax move is roughly a wash or even slightly in your favor. What actually eats the raise is the Bay Area's cost of living — mainly housing. A comparable 2-bedroom runs about $1,670/month more in SF than Portland, and overall cost of living is modeled at roughly 34% higher. Net it all out and you're looking at something like **$43K–$50K/year of genuinely added purchasing power for you individually** — real, but about a third smaller than the headline number, and that's *before* you've seen the actual vesting schedule on the equity (if a chunk of that $70K is stock that vests over four years, "today's" gain is smaller still).

Here's the thing, though: that math is almost beside the point. Once I ran the numbers, the dominant variable in this whole decision isn't your raise at all — it's what happens to your partner's income. A typical professional income lost or restarted from scratch will very plausibly swamp your $43–50K gain by itself. So the household-level verdict hinges almost entirely on one unanswered question: is "no remote option" a real, permanent constraint on the *field*, or just a fact about their current employer that might not hold for a Bay-Area-equivalent job?

There's a second thing worth naming: the "3 days a week" part of this deal isn't as stable as it looks. The whole Bay Area is trending toward *more* in-office time, not less — Amazon's at 5 days, a majority of Bay Area workers are now back full-time, and plenty of companies have walked back hybrid policies within a year or two of announcing them. If you relocate on the assumption that 3 days/week is the ceiling, and it quietly becomes 5, you've converted a "hybrid" decision into a full-relocation decision retroactively — after your partner's sacrifice is already sunk and much harder to undo.

When I actually scored the realistic paths against each other — accept as-is, decline, negotiate for remote/reduced terms, a trial "commuter" arrangement where you relocate and your partner stays put for now, or decline-but-use-it-as-leverage for a counteroffer — accepting the offer exactly as given came out clearly weakest. It's the option with the least reversibility, the most partner-career risk, and the biggest quality-of-life hit, and that ranking held up no matter how I reweighted the criteria. The strongest opening move is to **try to negotiate** — remote work, a reduced cadence, or a delayed/trial start — since that captures almost all the upside with the least risk. If they say no, declining while explicitly using the offer to negotiate with your *current* employer is the next-best fallback. Jumping straight to "yes, let's move" is the one path that dominates nothing.

If you accept and it fails, the most common thread isn't the money — it's that no one agreed on a fallback plan before moving, so when things got hard there was no pre-agreed exit point. If you decline and *that* turns out to be the regret, it's usually because the counter-offer or negotiation was never actually attempted — you declined outright instead of testing whether a better deal was on the table. Both point the same direction: don't make this a silent, unilateral, binary call.

So — bottom line, as a starting point for a conversation with your partner, not a verdict: don't treat this as "move or don't." Try to negotiate the terms first. 1. **Is your partner's career actually non-portable** — meaning the work itself can't be done remotely or from the Bay Area at any comparable level — or has it just never been offered that way at their current job?
